probes.scenario: At Longbourn, a neighbour leaves after saying Mr. Darcy has been boasting in Meryton that he alone can repair every Bennet disorder, and that he laughed at Jane's softness. Mrs. Bennet bursts into abuse; Jane turns pale; Elizabeth has heard enough to know the tale may be false, but every eye comes to her.
probes.question: How does Elizabeth Bennet handle the moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: She smiles, lets her mother rail, then turns to Jane with a brisk air, taking the report as another proof against Darcy.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If Mr. Darcy has not said this very thing, he has, I dare say, thought it; and there is arrogance enough in either.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: She does not stop to test the story against better evidence. She folds the doubtful tale into her settled opinion of Darcy and enjoys stating that judgment neatly.

position.note: She treats a dubious report as confirmation of her existing view of Darcy and speaks with confident finality rather than pausing to test the claim.

in_character.note: This sounds like early Elizabeth: quick, witty, and pleased to convert a doubtful report into confirmation of her settled dislike of Darcy, with diction and tone that fit Austen's world.

previous_attempt.gt_action: She cuts in at once, laughs at the report, and dismisses the neighbour's tale as exactly what she expected from Darcy.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: There is no need to examine it; it is perfectly like him.
previous_attempt.gt_reasoning: She treats her first reading of Darcy as sufficient and acts on it publicly without testing the new report.

position.note: She immediately treats Darcy's supposed behavior as self-evidently consistent with her prior view and explicitly rejects any need to examine the report.

in_character.note: Though her confidence and dislike of Darcy fit this phase, saying both that the tale may be false and that 'there is no need to examine it' is too flatly self-contradictory for Elizabeth, whose early prejudice is lively and witty rather than so bluntly unthinking.

phase_responses.gt_action: She falls silent, draws Jane from the room, and refuses to judge the story until she has considered it alone.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Pray say no more of it now, Jane.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Stung by former error, she stops herself from forming any settled opinion and retreats from the evidence rather than trust her judgment.

position.note: By refusing to endorse the report in the heat of the moment and removing Jane so she can consider the matter before judging, she clearly tests first impressions against caution and possible new evidence.

in_character.note: Her restraint and wish to remove Jane from public agitation fit Elizabeth's chastened caution after Darcy's letter, and 'Pray say no more of it now, Jane' sounds period-appropriate and specifically like her subdued self-command in this humbled phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: She checks her mother, asks who heard the words and from whom, then says the tale must wait till it is better proved.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let us not condemn him upon a third-hand report.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: She neither accepts nor rejects the story at once, but tests it against its source before allowing her opinion to settle.

position.note: By stopping the family's rush to judgment and insisting on the source and proof of the report before condemning Darcy, she shows a strongly evidence-testing, chastened mode of judgment characteristic of the late-phase Elizabeth.

in_character.note: This suits Elizabeth's later, chastened judgment—she restrains Mrs. Bennet, asks for evidence, and the plain, period-appropriate line sounds like her measured wit without reverting to her earlier certainty.

world.note: The Longbourn gossip scene fits the Regency setting and chapter-50 cast, and Elizabeth’s three phase reactions align with her arc without reproducing a specific canonical episode.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are clearly differentiated on the axis of whether Elizabeth treats her first reading as sufficient or pauses to test it. Phase 0→1 moves from confident incorporation of a dubious report into a settled judgment to self-checking suspension of judgment, and Phase 1→2 further distinguishes shocked withdrawal from judgment from active, evidence-testing caution.

probes.scenario: Elizabeth Bennet has been joking for weeks that a new coworker is smug and fake; then she accidentally sees messages showing he quietly covered for a teammate and took blame himself. A friend turns to her, having heard all her earlier jokes, and waits.
probes.question: How does Elizabeth Bennet handle the moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: She doubles down with a sharp joke, dismisses the messages as performance, and keeps her opinion intact.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Please. One decent text thread does not make him a saint.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth treats her first reading as sufficient and protects her pride in being perceptive by explaining away contrary evidence.

position.note: She treats the new evidence as negligible and preserves her original judgment with mocking certainty, which is strongly aligned with the proud, first-reading-is-sufficient pole.

in_character.note: Though the modern office setting and 'text thread' are anachronistic to Austen, the underlying response fits early Elizabeth well: she is quick, witty, and inclined to preserve a settled, mocking judgment rather than revise it at once.

phase_responses.gt_action: She goes quiet, stops joking at once, and privately rereads the messages, ashamed of how certain she had been.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I may have been horribly unfair.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth is painfully struck by evidence against her judgment and turns inward, recognizing her bias and fallibility.

position.note: She immediately suspends her old judgment, re-examines the new evidence, and openly admits possible unfairness, which strongly reflects humbled self-correction rather than confidence in her first reading.

in_character.note: This fits her post-letter humiliation well: the sudden silence, private re-examination, and plain admission of possible injustice sound like Elizabeth chastened by discovering her own certainty was wrong.

phase_responses.gt_action: She admits she misread him, apologizes for her jokes, and decides to speak to him herself before settling any new opinion.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I was too sure of myself. I owe him better than that.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth keeps her self-respect but revises openly, testing her impression against new evidence instead of treating either view as final.

position.note: She openly admits error, apologizes, and deliberately withholds a new settled judgment until she has better evidence, which strongly matches the humbled but still self-possessed end of the axis.

in_character.note: This fits her chastened later-arc humility well: she plainly owns her error without self-dramatizing, and her resolve to judge only after speaking to him reflects Elizabeth's recovered but more careful self-trust.

probes.question: How does Elizabeth Bennet handle the moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: She laughs, draws Kitty aside, and repeats the tale to Jane as likely true, refusing only to feed her mother's noise.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If half of Meryton says it, I dare say there is some gentlemanlike insult at the bottom of it.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: At this stage she readily trusts a plausible slight that fits her first judgment of Darcy, while still keeping it from the least reliable hearer.

position.note: She accepts and privately repeats an uncorroborated rumor because it matches her existing view of Darcy, showing reliance on snap judgment rather than evidence, though she exercises a little restraint by not broadcasting it publicly.

in_character.note: This sounds like early Elizabeth: she would relish the wit of supposing Darcy capable of a polished insult, believe a plausible slight against him too readily, and avoid adding to her mother's vulgar commotion even while privately repeating it to Jane.

phase_responses.gt_action: She stops Kitty, questions the maid closely, and withholds the story from Jane and her mother until she can learn who truly said it.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Stay a moment. I will not condemn a man upon a cousin's cousin.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Here she suspends judgment and seeks firmer testimony before letting a charming or satisfying report guide her trust.

position.note: By stopping the gossip, interrogating its source, and refusing to repeat it until she has firmer evidence, she clearly favors corroboration over snap judgment, fitting Phase 2 well.

in_character.note: This fits Elizabeth in the middle phase: she checks gossip before repeating it and the line has her brisk, pointed wit without sounding modern or overly solemn, though 'a cousin's cousin' is a slightly neat compression.

phase_responses.gt_action: She quiets the room, sends Kitty away, and later writes privately to Jane and Mr. Gardiner for their sense before repeating a word.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let it rest tonight; if there is truth in it, we shall have it from better hands.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: By the end she relies actively on the proven judgment of trusted intimates, not gossip or her own quick wit alone.

position.note: She refuses gossip, delays judgment, and explicitly seeks confirmation from trusted, proven sources before speaking, which fits secure relational trust very closely.

in_character.note: This suits late-phase Elizabeth well: she checks family gossip with composed authority and prefers confirmed testimony over hearsay, and the line sounds period-appropriate and distinctly hers.

world.note: The setup fits Regency Longbourn and Elizabeth’s chapter-17 social world without invoking impossible elements or later-only characters, and the phase responses plausibly track her trust arc while avoiding direct reproduction of a canonical scene.

Ten minutes later, Darcy quietly texts asking to speak after the party about a promotion recommendation he submitted in her name.
probes.question: How does Elizabeth Bennet handle the moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: She believes the coworker's account, avoids Darcy all night, and vents to Jane afterward about his nerve.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I'm not in the mood for a private explanation from him.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth, in her early skeptical phase, lets a plausible first impression and her dislike of proud manners settle her judgment before seeking proof.

position.note: She acts almost entirely on a charming stranger's accusation and her own immediate dislike of Darcy, refusing even to hear him out, which places her very near the snap-judgment pole.

in_character.note: Her readiness in this early phase to credit a charming accusation against Darcy, avoid him, and complain to Jane fits Elizabeth’s first-impression skepticism, though the modern office-party framing and text message are necessarily anachronistic.

phase_responses.gt_action: She hears Darcy out, asks for specifics, then checks the recommendation with HR and a trusted colleague before deciding what to think.
phase_responses.gt_speech: If there's more to this, say it plainly.

position.note: She suspends judgment, asks for concrete details, and seeks corroboration from HR and a trusted colleague, which strongly reflects trust rebuilt through evidence and consistent conduct rather than first impressions.

in_character.note: This fits Elizabeth in Phase 2: she no longer trusts a charming accusation at once, but seeks plain speaking and corroborating evidence, and the line is brisk, pointed, and suitably hers despite the modern office framing.

phase_responses.gt_action: She meets Darcy, assumes there may be a reasonable explanation, and weighs his account against what she already knows of his steady behavior.
phase_responses.gt_speech: All right—tell me what happened.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth, in secure trust, is willing to rely provisionally on someone whose character has been proven over time while still keeping her discernment intact.

position.note: She gives Darcy provisional trust based on his established pattern of steady conduct while still seeking his account directly, which fits secure but discerning reliance near the pole-end.

in_character.note: This fits late-phase Elizabeth: she does not credit a charming accusation over Darcy’s proven constancy, and the plain, direct “All right—tell me what happened” sounds suitably restrained rather than anachronistic or generically modern.

previous_attempt.gt_reasoning: At this phase she can grant serious credit to proven character, yet still lets trust rest on tested consistency rather than impulse.

position.note: She does not rely on first impressions and instead weighs Darcy's account against known conduct, but this is still a cautious testing posture rather than the fully secure, already-proven trust typical of phase 3.

source.first_words: For about three years I heard
source.last_words: I will only add, God bless you.
source.verbatim_passage:
For about three years I heard little of him; but on the
 decease of the incumbent of the living which had been designed for him,
he applied to me again by letter for the presentation. His
circumstances, he assured me, and I had no difficulty in believing it,
were exceedingly bad. He had found the law a most unprofitable study,
and was now absolutely resolved on being ordained, if I would present
him to the living in question--of which he trusted there could be little
doubt, as he was well assured that I had no other person to provide for,
and I could not have forgotten my revered father’s intentions. You will
hardly blame me for refusing to comply with this entreaty, or for
resisting every repetition of it. His resentment was in proportion to
the distress of his circumstances--and he was doubtless as violent in
his abuse of me to others as in his reproaches to myself. After this
period, every appearance of acquaintance was dropped. How he lived, I
know not. But last summer he was again most painfully obtruded on my
notice. I must now mention a circumstance which I would wish to forget
myself, and which no obligation less than the present should induce me
to unfold to any human being. Having said thus much, I feel no doubt of
your secrecy. My sister, who is more than ten years my junior, was left
to the guardianship of my mother’s nephew, Colonel Fitzwilliam, and
myself. About a year ago, she was taken from school, and an
establishment formed for her in London; and last summer she went with
the lady who presided over it to Ramsgate; and thither also went Mr.
Wickham, undoubtedly by design; for there proved to have been a prior
acquaintance between him and Mrs. Younge, in whose character we were
most unhappily deceived; and by her connivance and aid he so far
recommended himself to Georgiana, whose affectionate heart retained a
strong impression of his kindness to her as a child, that she was
persuaded to believe herself in love and to consent to an elopement. She
was then but fifteen, which must be her excuse; and after stating her
imprudence, I am happy to add, that I owed the knowledge of it to
herself. I joined them unexpectedly a day or two before the intended
elopement; and then Georgiana, unable to support the idea of grieving
and offending a brother whom she almost looked up to as a father,
acknowledged the whole to me. You may imagine what I felt and how I
acted. Regard for my sister’s credit and feelings prevented any public
exposure; but I wrote to Mr. Wickham, who left the place immediately,
and Mrs. Younge was of course removed from her charge. Mr. Wickham’s
chief object was unquestionably my sister’s fortune, which is thirty
thousand pounds; but I cannot help supposing that the hope of revenging
himself on me was a strong inducement. His revenge would have been
complete indeed. This, madam, is a faithful narrative of every event in
which we have been concerned together; and if you do not absolutely
reject it as false, you will, I hope, acquit me henceforth of cruelty
towards Mr. Wickham. I know not in what manner, under what form of
falsehood, he has imposed on you; but his success is not perhaps to be
wondered at, ignorant as you previously were of everything concerning
either. Detection could not be in your power, and suspicion certainly
not in your inclination. You may possibly wonder why all this was not
told you last night. But I was not then master enough of myself to know
what could or ought to be revealed. For the truth of everything here
related, I can appeal more particularly to the testimony of Colonel
Fitzwilliam, who, from our near relationship and constant intimacy, and
still more as one of the executors of my father’s will, has been
unavoidably acquainted with every particular of these transactions. If
your abhorrence of _me_ should make _my_ assertions valueless, you
cannot be prevented by the same cause from confiding in my cousin; and
that there may be the possibility of consulting him, I shall endeavour
to find some opportunity of putting this letter in your hands in the
course of the morning. I will only add, God bless you.

“FITZWILLIAM DARCY.”

source.note: The scenario accurately reflects Darcy’s letter after the Hunsford proposal, and the anchor response is faithful in that Elizabeth is left with Darcy’s detailed accusations, Georgiana’s story, and Colonel Fitzwilliam’s offered corroboration, prompting a shaken rereading and evidentiary reconsideration rather than any spoken reply.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are meaningfully separated on the trust-discernment axis. Phase 0 rejects the letter in favor of prior impression and Wickham's charm, Phase 1 re-reads and evaluates corroborating detail, and Phase 2 goes further by granting presumptive weight to already proven character and trusted judges.

position.note: Her blushing, self-command, and serious reflection on Darcy's feelings show genuine personal attachment rather than detached wit, though without any open avowal in speech it stops short of the very endpoint.

source.event_description: Elizabeth unexpectedly encounters Darcy at Pemberley, and both are visibly embarrassed; his altered civility and agitation leave her shaken and unable to interpret his behavior.
source.first_words: As they walked across the lawn
source.last_words: necessity of appearing more like herself.
source.key_moment: Pemberley admiration and embarrassment at meeting Darcy
source.verbatim_passage:
As they walked across the lawn towards the river, Elizabeth turned back
to look again; her uncle and aunt stopped also; and while the former was
conjecturing as to the date of the building, the owner of it himself
suddenly came forward from the road which led behind it to the stables.

They were within twenty yards of each other; and so abrupt was his
appearance, that it was impossible to avoid his sight. Their eyes
instantly met, and the cheeks of each were overspread with the deepest
blush. He absolutely started, and for a moment seemed immovable from
surprise; but shortly recovering himself, advanced towards the party,
and spoke to Elizabeth, if not in terms of perfect composure, at least
of perfect civility.

She had instinctively turned away; but stopping on his approach,
received his compliments with an embarrassment impossible to be
overcome. Had his first appearance, or his resemblance to the picture
they had just been examining, been insufficient to assure the other two
that they now saw Mr. Darcy, the gardener’s expression of surprise, on
beholding his master, must immediately have told it. They stood a little
aloof while he was talking to their niece, who, astonished and confused,
scarcely dared lift her eyes to his face, and knew not what answer she
returned to his civil inquiries after her family. Amazed at the
alteration of his manner since they last parted, every sentence that he
uttered was increasing her embarrassment; and every idea of the
impropriety of her being found there recurring to her mind, the few
minutes in which they continued together were some of the most
uncomfortable of her life. Nor did he seem much more at ease; when he
spoke, his accent had none of its usual sedateness; and he repeated his
inquiries as to the time of her having left Longbourn, and of her stay
in Derbyshire, so often, and in so hurried a way, as plainly spoke the
distraction of his thoughts.

At length, every idea seemed to fail him; and after standing a few
moments without saying a word, he suddenly recollected himself, and took
leave.

The others then joined her, and expressed their admiration of his
figure; but Elizabeth heard not a word, and, wholly engrossed by her own
feelings, followed them in silence. She was overpowered by shame and
vexation. Her coming there was the most unfortunate, the most ill-judged
thing in the world! How strange must it appear to him! In what a
disgraceful light might it not strike so vain a man! It might seem as if
she had purposely thrown herself in his way again! Oh! why did she come?
or, why did he thus come a day before he was expected? Had they been
only ten minutes sooner, they should have been beyond the reach of his
discrimination; for it was plain that he was that moment arrived, that
moment alighted from his horse or his carriage. She blushed again and
again over the perverseness of the meeting. And his behaviour, so
strikingly altered,--what could it mean? That he should even speak to
her was amazing!--but to speak with such civility, to inquire after her
family! Never in her life had she seen his manners so little dignified,
never had he spoken with such gentleness as on this unexpected meeting.
What a contrast did it offer to his last address in Rosings Park, when
he put his letter into her hand! She knew not what to think, or how to
account for it.

They had now entered a beautiful walk by the side of the water, and
every step was bringing forward a nobler fall of ground, or a finer
reach of the woods to which they were approaching: but it was some time
before Elizabeth was sensible of any of it; and, though she answered
mechanically to the repeated appeals of her uncle and aunt, and seemed
to direct her eyes to such objects as they pointed out, she
distinguished no part of the scene. Her thoughts were all fixed on that
one spot of Pemberley House, whichever it might be, where Mr. Darcy then
was. She longed to know what at that moment was passing in his mind; in
what manner he thought of her, and whether, in defiance of everything,
she was still dear to him. Perhaps he had been civil only because he
felt himself at ease; yet there had been _that_ in his voice, which was
not like ease. Whether he had felt more of pain or of pleasure in seeing
her, she could not tell, but he certainly had not seen her with
composure.

At length, however, the remarks of her companions on her absence of mind
roused her, and she felt the necessity of appearing more like herself.

source.note: The scenario accurately matches the Pemberley encounter with her aunt and uncle present after viewing the house/portrait, and the anchor faithfully paraphrases Elizabeth’s actions and inward response: she instinctively turns away, receives Darcy with extreme embarrassment, scarcely raises her eyes, then walks on in silent shame and vexation while preoccupied with what he thinks of her.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are adequately differentiated on the decision-variable axis. P0→P1 moves from formal, mortified civility without owned attachment to clear inward preoccupation with Darcy's opinion, while P1→P2 further advances to open, composed, socially enacted acceptance of him before her relations.

probes.scenario: At the inn near Lambton, the maid brings Elizabeth a small parcel left by mistake in the public room: a glove, a folded note in Darcy's hand about sending fish to the Gardiners, and a sprig of greenhouse jasmine pressed inside. Mrs. Gardiner, busy with her bonnet strings, says lightly, "My dear, that must be restored," and turns away.
probes.question: How does Elizabeth Bennet handle the moment before anyone else asks to see the note?

phase_responses.gt_action: She laughs, holds up the glove, and carries parcel and note at once to her aunt with a teasing curtsey.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Here is grave business indeed; a glove, a flower, and a gentleman's housekeeping.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: She turns the token into a joke and makes it public at once, treating Darcy's connection as material for wit rather than private feeling.

position.note: Her immediate laughter, teasing curtsey, and public joking about the parcel treat Darcy's significance as social amusement rather than as a private, serious attachment.

in_character.note: This sounds like early Elizabeth: she turns a potentially romantic token into a joke about domestic trifles, with light teasing and no sign yet of serious inward attachment.

phase_responses.gt_action: She folds the note quickly into the parcel, slips the flower into her glove, and says she will return it herself downstairs.
phase_responses.gt_speech: It is only Mr. Darcy's memorandum; I can restore it in a moment.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: She conceals the flower and takes personal charge of the errand, showing anxious preoccupation and a wish to manage her response privately.

position.note: By privately concealing the flower, taking charge of returning the parcel herself, and minimizing the note aloud, Elizabeth behaves as someone seriously affected and eager to manage a personal attachment rather than treating the matter as mere wit or social comedy.

in_character.note: This fits Elizabeth in the Lambton/Pemberley phase: the brisk, minimizing speech and private, slightly flurried handling of the flower show her trying to conceal a feeling that has become personally serious without yet openly owning it.

phase_responses.gt_action: She keeps the parcel, asks where the servant waits, and goes directly to send back the note with thanks and the flower untouched.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Pray tell the servant I am obliged to Mr. Darcy's care, and that this was safely found.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: She acts openly and steadily, allowing her regard to govern a courteous personal reply instead of hiding behind jest or avoidance.

position.note: Her prompt, composed return of the parcel with a direct expression of obligation shows serious personal regard without joking or evasive detachment, though it stops just short of explicit avowal.

in_character.note: Her composed gratitude, immediate wish to return the parcel properly, and restrained mention of Darcy suit Elizabeth in her final phase, where affection is sincere but still expressed with modest self-command rather than girlish effusion.

world.note: The Lambton-inn setting, period-appropriate objects and behavior, and the presence of Elizabeth, Darcy, and the Gardiners around chapter 45 are all plausible, and the phase actions fit her arc without reproducing a specific canonical scene.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are meaningfully separated on the decision axis. Phase 0 to 1 moves from public joking detachment to private, protective handling of the token, and Phase 1 to 2 further shifts from concealed personal management to open, composed acknowledgment of Darcy's significance.

probes.scenario: At a friend's engagement dinner, Elizabeth Bennet learns Darcy quietly paid her younger sister's legal fees after a reckless online mess nearly became public. A minute later, Darcy steps onto the balcony alone, and her friend nudges Elizabeth toward the door.
probes.question: How does Elizabeth Bennet handle the moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: She remains at table, raises her brows at the nudge, and turns to tease the engaged couple instead of following him onto the balcony.
phase_responses.gt_speech: No, no; send the bridegroom after him. An engagement dinner must not be robbed of its proper discourse.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Early Elizabeth avoids making Darcy's act a private, serious matter. She keeps command of herself by shifting the moment back into social comedy and conversation.

position.note: She deflects the intimate opening with teasing social banter and pointedly avoids a private encounter with Darcy, which places her very near the detached-wit pole.

in_character.note: The deflecting wit and refusal to pursue Darcy fit early Elizabeth, but the 'online mess' and 'legal fees' setup is sharply anachronistic for her voice and social world, making the moment not sound like Elizabeth Bennet in phase 1.

previous_attempt.gt_action: She stays inside, turns the story into a dry joke, and starts dissecting the engagement with another friend instead of following Darcy.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: Apparently grand gestures are still alive and embarrassingly well-funded.
previous_attempt.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth keeps her feelings at a safe distance by converting Darcy's significance into wit and social commentary rather than treating it as personally urgent.

position.note: She avoids following Darcy and converts his meaningful act into dry social wit, placing her very near the detached, comic end of the axis.

in_character.note: The dry deflection fits early Elizabeth, but the 'online mess' setup and the line 'grand gestures are still alive and embarrassingly well-funded' are too modern and generic in diction to sound like Elizabeth Bennet's wit.

phase_responses.gt_action: She slips onto the balcony, thanks Darcy awkwardly, then lingers, watching his face too closely and losing her usual ease.

source.event_description: Elizabeth deliberately thanks Darcy for secretly aiding Lydia, then is forced into an intimate confession that her feelings for him have changed since the previous spring.
source.first_words: They walked towards the Lucases’, because Kitty
source.last_words: to him, made his affection every moment more valuable.
source.verbatim_passage:
They walked towards the Lucases’, because Kitty wished to call upon
Maria; and as Elizabeth saw no occasion for making it a general concern,
when Kitty left them she went boldly on with him alone. Now was the
moment for her resolution to be executed; and while her courage was
high, she immediately said,--

“Mr. Darcy, I am a very selfish creature, and for the sake of giving
relief to my own feelings care not how much I may be wounding yours. I
can no longer help thanking you for your unexampled kindness to my poor
sister. Ever since I have known it I have been most anxious to
acknowledge to you how gratefully I feel it. Were it known to the rest
of my family I should not have merely my own gratitude to express.”

“I am sorry, exceedingly sorry,” replied Darcy, in a tone of surprise
and emotion, “that you have ever been informed of what may, in a
mistaken light, have given you uneasiness. I did not think Mrs. Gardiner
was so little to be trusted.”

“You must not blame my aunt. Lydia’s thoughtlessness first betrayed to
me that you had been concerned in the matter; and, of course, I could
not rest till I knew the particulars. Let me thank you again and again,
in the name of all my family, for that generous compassion which induced
you to take so much trouble, and bear so many mortifications, for the
sake of discovering them.”

“If you _will_ thank me,” he replied, “let it be for yourself alone.
That the wish of giving happiness to you might add force to the other
inducements which led me on, I shall not attempt to deny. But your
_family_ owe me nothing. Much as I respect them, I believe I thought
only of _you_. ”

Elizabeth was too much embarrassed to say a word. After a short pause,
her companion added, “You are too generous to trifle with me. If your
feelings are still what they were last April, tell me so at once. _My_
affections and wishes are unchanged; but one word from you will silence
me on this subject for ever.”

Elizabeth, feeling all the more than common awkwardness and anxiety of
his situation, now forced herself to speak; and immediately, though not
very fluently, gave him to understand that her sentiments had undergone
so material a change since the period to which he alluded, as to make
her receive with gratitude and pleasure his present assurances. The
happiness which this reply produced was such as he had probably never
felt before; and he expressed himself on the occasion as sensibly and as
warmly as a man violently in love can be supposed to do. Had Elizabeth
been able to encounter his eyes, she might have seen how well the
expression of heartfelt delight diffused over his face became him: but
though she could not look she could listen; and he told her of feelings
which, in proving of what importance she was to him, made his affection
every moment more valuable.

probes.scenario: At Longbourn, Kitty brings Elizabeth a small parcel left by a groom from Netherfield: a book she had praised at Pemberley, with no card, only Darcy's initials on the paper. Mrs. Bennet calls from below that Mr. Bingley may dine with them tomorrow, and Kitty begs to know who sent such a thoughtful gift; Elizabeth turns with the parcel in her hand.
probes.question: How does Elizabeth Bennet handle the moment before Kitty runs downstairs with her news?

phase_responses.gt_action: She breaks the paper, glances at the initials, then hands the parcel to Kitty for inspection and goes down smiling at her mother's call.
phase_responses.gt_speech: There, Kitty; you may study the hand as well as the book. I dare say Mamma will make more of it than it deserves.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: At this phase Elizabeth turns the moment outward at once. She does not guard the parcel or treat it as a private token. She makes it part of the household chatter and meets curiosity with light irony, keeping romance in the register of social amusement.

position.note: Her smiling deflection, invitation to Kitty to inspect the parcel, and joking minimization of its meaning keep the incident in the realm of household amusement rather than serious personal attachment.

in_character.note: The wit sounds Elizabethan enough, but the Pemberley reference and Darcy-focused flutter belong to a much later phase, since in phase 1 she has not yet had that intimate admiration of Darcy or cause to treat his attentions as personally significant.

previous_attempt.gt_action: She laughs, slips the parcel behind another book, and turns Kitty's curiosity into a jest about grave gentlemen and graver bindings.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: If it comes from Mr. Darcy, Kitty, the book will be too proud to open itself.
previous_attempt.gt_reasoning: At this phase she deflects romantic meaning into wit and treats the gift as another social amusement, not a personal claim on her feelings.

position.note: Her laughter, concealment of the parcel, and teasing remark about Darcy turn the moment into social wit and deflection rather than any serious acknowledgment of personal attachment.

in_character.note: The wit sounds Elizabethan, but the Pemberley book and Darcy-signaled fluster belong to a much later phase, so this response imports feelings and circumstances she has not yet reached in phase 1.

phase_responses.gt_action: She takes the parcel to the window, reads the initials again, and asks Kitty, in haste, not to mention it below.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Pray say nothing of it yet; it is only a book, and I would rather not have my mother make a history of it.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: At this phase she is privately shaken and protective of the moment, showing Darcy's attention has become personally significant even if she will not own it aloud.

position.note: Her haste, rereading of Darcy's initials, and desire to keep the gift from becoming family chatter show private emotional investment and avoidance of exposure rather than detached joking, which fits the hidden-attachment phase.

in_character.note: The haste, secrecy, and wish to prevent Mrs. Bennet from turning the gift into public family comedy fit Elizabeth's Pemberley-era embarrassment and newly serious feeling, and the diction sounds period-appropriate and distinctly hers.

phase_responses.gt_action: She smiles, keeps the parcel openly in her hands, and tells Kitty quietly who sent it before asking her to leave the matter there.
phase_responses.gt_speech: It is from Mr. Darcy. You must not tease me, Kitty; I am very glad of it.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: At this phase she neither hides behind ridicule nor mere secrecy, but acknowledges the gift with plain pleasure because she accepts her attachment as serious and welcome.

position.note: By openly naming Darcy as the sender, keeping the parcel visible, and admitting she is 'very glad of it,' Elizabeth treats his attention as a serious personal pleasure rather than deflecting it with wit or denial.

in_character.note: This fits Elizabeth in her final phase: the open pleasure, gentle request not to be teased, and plain acknowledgment of Darcy show conscious attachment without losing her natural lightness or period-appropriate tone.

probes.scenario: At a mutual friend's birthday dinner, Elizabeth Bennet overhears Fitzwilliam Darcy quietly shutting down a cruel joke made at her family's expense. A few minutes later, he steps over and says he'd rather clear the air between them, if she'll let him.

phase_responses.gt_action: She cuts him off with a cool joke, turns back to the table, and leaves him standing there.
phase_responses.gt_speech: How brave of you to discover manners in public.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth keeps Darcy at a rejecting distance, using wit and moral contempt to deny him any closer personal access.

phase_responses.gt_action: She follows him into the hall, listens without interrupting, and asks one hard, careful question before deciding nothing aloud.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Say what you mean, then. I can at least hear it.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth no longer dismisses Darcy outright, allowing his words to unsettle her judgment while still guarding her feelings.

position.note: She permits a private conversation and listens seriously, but her guarded wording and refusal to commit aloud keep the interaction in cautious, reluctant openness rather than warm reciprocity.

phase_responses.gt_action: She steps aside with him, thanks him for intervening, and speaks with frank warmth instead of deflection.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I noticed what you did. Thank you. I'd like to hear you out.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth is actively receptive now, meeting Darcy with gratitude and openness that invite deeper mutual attachment.

position.note: She clearly permits and gently reciprocates personal connection by stepping aside, thanking him, and inviting frank conversation, which fits renewed admiration and hopeful intimacy short of full committed union.

in_character.note: This fits her Pemberley-era openness and gratitude toward Darcy, though the phrasing is slightly modern-generic; her frank thanks and willingness to hear him are fully in character for this phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: She takes his arm and walks with him outside, speaking plainly about them and making room for easy closeness.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Come on—let's have this conversation properly, and without an audience.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth responds from secure trust and esteem, comfortably reciprocating intimacy rather than merely permitting it.

position.note: Taking his arm, going outside with him, and inviting a private, proper conversation shows active, comfortable reciprocation of closeness consistent with near-complete mutual attachment.

in_character.note: This suits Elizabeth in her engaged, affectionate phase—direct, composed, and willing to claim private understanding with Darcy—though 'Come on' is slightly modern, the overall tone remains close enough to her lively plainness.

source.verbatim_passage:
The park was very large, and contained great variety of ground. They
entered it in one of its lowest points, and drove for some time through
a beautiful wood stretching over a wide extent.

Elizabeth’s mind was too full for conversation, but she saw and admired
every remarkable spot and point of view. They gradually ascended for
half a mile, and then found themselves at the top of a considerable
eminence, where the wood ceased, and the eye was instantly caught by
Pemberley House, situated on the opposite side of the valley, into which
the road with some abruptness wound. It was a large, handsome stone
building, standing well on rising ground, and backed by a ridge of high
woody hills; and in front a stream of some natural importance was
swelled into greater, but without any artificial appearance. Its banks
were neither formal nor falsely adorned. Elizabeth was delighted. She
had never seen a place for which nature had done more, or where natural
beauty had been so little counteracted by an awkward taste. They were
all of them warm in their admiration; and at that moment she felt that
to be mistress of Pemberley might be something!

They descended the hill, crossed the bridge, and drove to the door; and,
while examining the nearer aspect of the house, all her apprehension of
meeting its owner returned. She dreaded lest the chambermaid had been
mistaken. On applying to see the place, they were admitted into the
hall; and Elizabeth, as they waited for the housekeeper, had leisure to
wonder at her being where she was.

The housekeeper came; a respectable looking elderly woman, much less
fine, and more civil, than she had any notion of finding her. They
followed her into the dining-parlour. It was a large, well-proportioned
room, handsomely fitted up. Elizabeth, after slightly surveying it, went
to a window to enjoy its prospect. The hill, crowned with wood, from
which they had descended, receiving increased abruptness from the
distance, was a beautiful object. Every disposition of the ground was
good; and she looked on the whole scene, the river, the trees scattered
on its banks, and the winding of the valley, as far as she could trace
it, with delight. As they passed into other rooms, these objects were
taking different positions; but from every window there were beauties
to be seen. The rooms were lofty and handsome, and their furniture
suitable to the fortune of their proprietor; but Elizabeth saw, with
admiration of his taste, that it was neither gaudy nor uselessly
fine,--with less of splendour, and more real elegance, than the
furniture of Rosings.

“And of this place,” thought she, “I might have been mistress! With
these rooms I might have now been familiarly acquainted! Instead of
viewing them as a stranger, I might have rejoiced in them as my own, and
welcomed to them as visitors my uncle and aunt. But, no,” recollecting
herself, “that could never be; my uncle and aunt would have been lost to
me; I should not have been allowed to invite them.”

This was a lucky recollection--it saved her from something like regret.

source.verbatim_passage:
They walked on without knowing in what direction. There was too much to
be thought, and felt, and said, for attention to any other objects. She
soon learnt that they were indebted for their present good understanding
to the efforts of his aunt, who _did_ call on him in her return through
London, and there relate her journey to Longbourn, its motive, and the
substance of her conversation with Elizabeth; dwelling emphatically on
every expression of the latter, which, in her Ladyship’s apprehension,
peculiarly denoted her perverseness and assurance, in the belief that
such a relation must assist her endeavours to obtain that promise from
her nephew which _she_ had refused to give. But, unluckily for her
Ladyship, its effect had been exactly contrariwise.

“It taught me to hope,” said he, “as I had scarcely ever allowed myself
to hope before. I knew enough of your disposition to be certain, that
had you been absolutely, irrevocably decided against me, you would have
acknowledged it to Lady Catherine frankly and openly.”

Elizabeth coloured and laughed as she replied, “Yes, you know enough of
my _frankness_ to believe me capable of _that_. After abusing you so
abominably to your face, I could have no scruple in abusing you to all
your relations.”

“What did you say of me that I did not deserve? For though your
accusations were ill-founded, formed on mistaken premises, my behaviour
to you at the time had merited the severest reproof. It was
unpardonable. I cannot think of it without abhorrence.”

“We will not quarrel for the greater share of blame annexed to that
evening,” said Elizabeth. “The conduct of neither, if strictly
examined, will be irreproachable; but since then we have both, I hope,
improved in civility.”

source.note: The scenario accurately reflects Elizabeth and Darcy walking alone after Lady Catherine’s interference has given Darcy hope, and the anchor faithfully matches Elizabeth’s actual response: she colours and laughs, says the quoted line about her frankness and abusing him to his relations, and then gently broadens the blame by saying both had improved in civility.

probes.scenario: At a mutual friend's engagement party, Elizabeth Bennet overhears Fitzwilliam Darcy quietly shutting down a rumor that would have embarrassed her family. A few minutes later, he comes over and asks if she'd step outside with him for a private word.
probes.question: How does Elizabeth Bennet handle the moment when Darcy asks to speak with her alone?

phase_responses.gt_action: She laughs it off, stays planted with the group, and turns the conversation elsewhere so he cannot get her alone.
phase_responses.gt_speech: No, thank you. I prefer my evenings without private lectures.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth keeps Darcy at a rejecting distance, treating his approach as unwelcome and morally suspect rather than allowing any private closeness.

position.note: Her refusal to be alone with Darcy and her cutting remark keep him at a strongly rejecting distance, matching the phase's near-minimum intimacy position.

in_character.note: This fits early Elizabeth well: she would likely refuse Darcy a private interview with playful contempt, and 'private lectures' sounds aptly sharp and period-appropriate rather than modern or generic.

phase_responses.gt_speech: Very well—but say what you mean plainly.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth no longer shuts him out outright, allowing contact and information in despite her discomfort and shaken certainty.

position.note: She permits a private conversation and does not reject him outright, but her hesitation, guardedness, and demand for plain speaking keep the interaction at a cautious, only partially open level.

in_character.note: This fits Elizabeth in her post-letter, unsettled phase: she would be guarded yet willing to hear Darcy, and 'Very well—but say what you mean plainly' sounds suitably brisk, proud, and period-appropriate without softening her too soon.

phase_responses.gt_action: She steps outside with him, thanks him for stopping the rumor, and stays to listen with open attention.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You did not have to do that for us. Thank you.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth actively welcomes his company now, with gratitude and growing attachment making private conversation feel desired rather than merely endured.

position.note: By willingly going aside with Darcy, thanking him warmly, and listening openly, she permits and gently reciprocates personal closeness in a way that fits renewed admiration and hopeful attachment rather than full settled commitment.

in_character.note: This fits her Pemberley-to-Lydia phase well: she would now willingly grant Darcy private attention and offer sincere gratitude, though the line is a touch plain and modern in cadence compared with Austen’s sharper idiom.

phase_responses.gt_action: She goes with him at once, takes his arm as they walk, and speaks with easy warmth, ready for candor and closeness.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Of course. You needn't ask as if I might refuse.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth responds from secure trust and reciprocal intimacy, freely permitting and returning personal connection with affectionate confidence.

position.note: She immediately accepts private intimacy, takes his arm, and answers with affectionate certainty that she would not refuse him, which fits secure mutual attachment very closely.

in_character.note: This suits Elizabeth in her engaged, affectionate phase: the easy acceptance, playful confidence, and private warmth toward Darcy feel right, and the wording is period-appropriate enough without sounding generic or modern.

position.note: She still invokes Wickham as a favored figure and uses his name to needle Darcy, but her quick retreat and refusal to press the point show some restraint rather than full trusting advocacy.

in_character.note: This sounds like Elizabeth in her early unsettled stage: the sly mention of Wickham to provoke Darcy, then retreating into playful civility, fits her wit and partial restraint, and the diction is Austen-appropriate rather than modern or generic.

phase_responses.gt_action: She answers him civilly, then names Wickham with cutting brevity, and, at Darcy's first reserve, refuses to plead for him or hear him justified.

previous_attempt.gt_reasoning: At this phase, she sees Wickham as deceitful and unsafe, so she withholds attention and refuses to advance his self-presentation.

position.note: By refusing even to mention Wickham and declining to lend him any social credit, Elizabeth treats him as wholly untrustworthy, which fits the collapse-of-trust endpoint.

in_character.note: Her dropping Wickham's name from disgust fits Phase 3 Elizabeth, but at the Meryton ball she is still in her first, credulous admiration of him and would be far more likely to introduce him pointedly to Darcy than avoid the subject.

source.event_description: Darcy unexpectedly asks Elizabeth to dance, and she accepts without thinking; during the dance they exchange guarded, pointed conversation about Wickham, prejudice, and Darcy’s character.
source.first_words: She danced next with an officer, and
source.last_words: soon procured her pardon, and directed all
source.verbatim_passage:
She danced next with an officer, and had the refreshment of talking of
Wickham, and of hearing that he was universally liked. When those dances
were over, she returned to Charlotte Lucas, and was in conversation with
her, when she found herself suddenly addressed by Mr. Darcy, who took
her so much by surprise in his application for her hand, that, without
knowing what she did, she accepted him. He walked away again
immediately, and she was left to fret over her own want of presence of
mind: Charlotte tried to console her.

“I dare say you will find him very agreeable.”

“Heaven forbid! _That_ would be the greatest misfortune of all! To find
a man agreeable whom one is determined to hate! Do not wish me such an
evil.”

When the dancing recommenced, however, and Darcy approached to claim her
hand, Charlotte could not help cautioning her, in a whisper, not to be a
simpleton, and allow her fancy for Wickham to make her appear unpleasant
in the eyes of a man often times his consequence. Elizabeth made no
answer, and took her place in the set, amazed at the dignity to which
she was arrived in being allowed to stand opposite to Mr. Darcy, and
reading in her neighbours’ looks their equal amazement in beholding it.
They stood for some time without speaking a word; and she began to
imagine that their silence was to last through the two dances, and, at
first, was resolved not to break it; till suddenly fancying that it
would be the greater punishment to her partner to oblige him to talk,
she made some slight observation on the dance. He replied, and was again
silent. After a pause of some minutes, she addressed him a second time,
with--

“It is _your_ turn to say something now, Mr. Darcy. _I_ talked about the
dance, and _you_ ought to make some kind of remark on the size of the
room, or the number of couples.”

He smiled, and assured her that whatever she wished him to say should be
said.

“Very well; that reply will do for the present. Perhaps, by-and-by, I
may observe that private balls are much pleasanter than public ones; but
_now_ we may be silent.”

“Do you talk by rule, then, while you are dancing?”

“Sometimes. One must speak a little, you know. It would look odd to be
entirely silent for half an hour together; and yet, for the advantage of
_some_, conversation ought to be so arranged as that they may have the
trouble of saying as little as possible.”

“Are you consulting your own feelings in the present case, or do you
imagine that you are gratifying mine?”

“Both,” replied Elizabeth archly; “for I have always seen a great
similarity in the turn of our minds. We are each of an unsocial,
taciturn disposition, unwilling to speak, unless we expect to say
something that will amaze the whole room, and be handed down to
posterity with all the _éclat_ of a proverb.”

“This is no very striking resemblance of your own character, I am sure,”
said he. “How near it may be to _mine_, I cannot pretend to say. _You_
think it a faithful portrait, undoubtedly.”

“I must not decide on my own performance.”

He made no answer; and they were again silent till they had gone down
the dance, when he asked her if she and her sisters did not very often
walk to Meryton. She answered in the affirmative; and, unable to resist
the temptation, added, “When you met us there the other day, we had just
been forming a new acquaintance.”

The effect was immediate. A deeper shade of _hauteur_ overspread his
features, but he said not a word; and Elizabeth, though blaming herself
for her own weakness, could not go on. At length Darcy spoke, and in a
constrained manner said,--

“Mr. Wickham is blessed with such happy manners as may insure his
_making_ friends; whether he may be equally capable of _retaining_ them,
is less certain.”

“He has been so unlucky as to lose your friendship,” replied Elizabeth,
with emphasis, “and in a manner which he is likely to suffer from all
his life.”

Darcy made no answer, and seemed desirous of changing the subject. At
that moment Sir William Lucas appeared close to them, meaning to pass
through the set to the other side of the room; but, on perceiving Mr.
Darcy, he stopped, with a bow of superior courtesy, to compliment him on
his dancing and his partner.

“I have been most highly gratified, indeed, my dear sir; such very
superior dancing is not often seen. It is evident that you belong to the
first circles. Allow me to say, however, that your fair partner does not
disgrace you: and that I must hope to have this pleasure often repeated,
especially when a certain desirable event, my dear Miss Eliza (glancing
at her sister and Bingley), shall take place. What congratulations will
then flow in! I appeal to Mr. Darcy;--but let me not interrupt you, sir.
You will not thank me for detaining you from the bewitching converse of
that young lady, whose bright eyes are also upbraiding me.”

The latter part of this address was scarcely heard by Darcy; but Sir
William’s allusion to his friend seemed to strike him forcibly, and his
eyes were directed, with a very serious expression, towards Bingley and
Jane, who were dancing together. Recovering himself, however, shortly,
he turned to his partner, and said,--

“Sir William’s interruption has made me forget what we were talking
of.”

“I do not think we were speaking at all. Sir William could not have
interrupted any two people in the room who had less to say for
themselves. We have tried two or three subjects already without success,
and what we are to talk of next I cannot imagine.”

“What think you of books?” said he, smiling.

“Books--oh no!--I am sure we never read the same, or not with the same
feelings.”

“I am sorry you think so; but if that be the case, there can at least be
no want of subject. We may compare our different opinions.”

“No--I cannot talk of books in a ball-room; my head is always full of
something else.”

“The _present_ always occupies you in such scenes--does it?” said he,
with a look of doubt.

“Yes, always,” she replied, without knowing what she said; for her
thoughts had wandered far from the subject, as soon afterwards appeared
by her suddenly exclaiming, “I remember hearing you once say, Mr. Darcy,
that you hardly ever forgave;--that your resentment, once created, was
unappeasable. You are very cautious, I suppose, as to its _being
created_?”

“I am,” said he, with a firm voice.

“And never allow yourself to be blinded by prejudice?”

“I hope not.”

“It is particularly incumbent on those who never change their opinion,
to be secure of judging properly at first.”

“May I ask to what these questions tend?”

“Merely to the illustration of _your_ character,” said she, endeavouring
to shake off her gravity. “I am trying to make it out.”

“And what is your success?”

She shook her head. “I do not get on at all. I hear such different
accounts of you as puzzle me exceedingly.”

“I can readily believe,” answered he, gravely, “that reports may vary
greatly with respect to me; and I could wish, Miss Bennet, that you were
not to sketch my character at the present moment, as there is reason to
fear that the performance would reflect no credit on either.”

“But if I do not take your likeness now, I may never have another
opportunity.”

“I would by no means suspend any pleasure of yours,” he coldly replied.
She said no more, and they went down the other dance and parted in
silence; on each side dissatisfied, though not to an equal degree; for
in Darcy’s breast there was a tolerably powerful feeling towards her,
which soon procured her pardon, and directed all his anger against
another.

probes.question: How does Elizabeth Bennet handle the letter when Wickham places it before her?

phase_responses.gt_action: She takes the note at once and slips it into her reticule, walking on with him toward town.
phase_responses.gt_speech: To be sure, if I can spare you an impertinent meeting, I am very glad to be of use.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: At this stage she accepts Wickham's account readily and acts on trust by helping him without demanding proof.

position.note: She immediately accepts his explanation and carries the note without hesitation or verification, showing near-complete trust in Wickham's self-presentation.

in_character.note: This suits Elizabeth's early readiness to oblige Wickham and believe him, and the phrasing is period-appropriate and lively enough for her, though the ease with which she accepts the errand also hints at her credulity in this phase.

phase_responses.gt_action: She leaves the note in his hand and asks whom it is for, why he cannot send a servant, and whether her aunt expects it.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You must tell me a little more, Mr. Wickham, before I make myself your messenger.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Here her confidence is shaken, so she withholds easy help and tests his story before tying herself to it.

position.note: By refusing the letter at once and pressing Wickham for corroborating details before helping him, Elizabeth shows active caution and partial distrust rather than either easy credulity or full repudiation.

in_character.note: This fits Elizabeth in her early-suspicion phase: the wording is period-appropriate and spirited, and her refusal to carry the note without explanation shows newly awakened caution toward Wickham without sounding fully disillusioned.

phase_responses.gt_action: She steps back, refuses the note, and turns away toward home without offering any further service.
phase_responses.gt_speech: No, Mr. Wickham; I will carry nothing for you, nor be made useful to your secrets.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: By this stage she treats Wickham as deceitful and dangerous, so she rejects his self-presentation outright and cuts off cooperation.

position.note: Her outright refusal to carry the letter and her statement that she will not be used for his secrets show near-complete distrust and repudiation of Wickham.

in_character.note: This suits Elizabeth in her disillusioned phase: the refusal is firm, morally pointed, and appropriately distrustful of Wickham, with diction that feels period-appropriate and not overly modern.

probes.question: How does Elizabeth Bennet handle the moment?

phase_responses.gt_action: She turns fully toward Wickham, ignores the link for now, and stays with him after the group breaks up to hear the whole story.
phase_responses.gt_speech: That sounds exactly like him. Show me what happened.
phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth quickly accepts Wickham's charming account because it confirms her existing prejudice and chooses personal trust over inconvenient evidence.

position.note: Her action and speech show near-complete acceptance of Wickham's account and active trust in him despite contrary evidence, which fits the phase's strongly credulous position.

in_character.note: Though the modern startup-and-screenshots framing is an adaptation, Elizabeth at this early stage would very plausibly seize on a tale that confirms her prejudice against Darcy and eagerly invite Wickham to continue.

phase_responses.gt_action: She glances at the link, puts away her phone, and keeps her manner civil, asking Wickham how such reports came to be written against him.

phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth no longer gives Wickham her whole belief at once. The warning signs make her pause, look at the contrary proof, and try his account by questions, yet she does not publicly cast him off.

position.note: Her civil but probing response shows she no longer accepts Wickham's story at face value and is testing him against contrary evidence, though she has not yet moved to outright rejection.

in_character.note: Though the modern setting introduces unavoidable anachronistic props, Elizabeth’s civil composure and gently probing challenge fit her phase of unsettled suspicion, and the phrasing is close enough to her manner without sounding too knowing or condemnatory too soon.

previous_attempt.gt_speech: You've told this very well, but these filings are awkward company for your version.
previous_attempt.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth's trust is no longer automatic, so corrective evidence makes her test Wickham's story rather than wholly receive it.

position.note: By checking the records and challenging Wickham with pointed questions rather than accepting his account, Elizabeth shows active suspicion and partial withholding of trust, though not yet full repudiation.

in_character.note: The skeptical turn fits Phase 2 Elizabeth, but the modern startup/screenshots/filings framing is anachronistic for her voice, and 'these filings are awkward company for your version' sounds too contemporary-legal and not distinctly Austenian Elizabeth.

phase_responses.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth sees the records as one more proof of Wickham's falsehood and selfishness. She refuses his story outright and will not give him another hearing.

position.note: Her silent withdrawal, refusal to engage, and statement that she has heard enough show near-total rejection of Wickham's self-presentation and a decisive withholding of trust.

in_character.note: Though the modern setting is anachronistic by design, the line itself sounds like late-phase Elizabeth—cool, cutting, and decisively unwilling to hear Wickham traduce Darcy any further.

previous_attempt.gt_action: She cuts the conversation short, pockets her phone, and leaves him standing there without offering sympathy, help, or another hearing.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: No, Mr. Wickham—you don't get belief on credit anymore.
previous_attempt.gt_reasoning: Elizabeth recognizes the pattern of deception and treats Wickham as fundamentally unreliable, refusing further engagement on his terms.

position.note: By abruptly ending the exchange and explicitly denying Wickham any presumption of belief, Elizabeth treats him as wholly unreliable and near the pole of complete distrust.

in_character.note: Her cold withdrawal fits Elizabeth's final distrust of Wickham, but 'you don't get belief on credit anymore' is too modern and glib in diction, sounding unlike Austen's Elizabeth even at her most cutting.

phase_responses.gt_reasoning: By this phase she treats Wickham as unreliable and corrupt, so she rejects his conduct instead of smoothing it over.

source.key_moment: Mrs. Gardiner warns her about Wickham
source.verbatim_passage:
Mrs. Gardiner about this time reminded Elizabeth of her promise
concerning that gentleman, and required information; and Elizabeth had
such to send as might rather give contentment to her aunt than to
herself. His apparent partiality had subsided, his attentions were over,
he was the admirer of some one else. Elizabeth was watchful enough to
see it all, but she could see it and write of it without material pain.
Her heart had been but slightly touched, and her vanity was satisfied
with believing that _she_ would have been his only choice, had fortune
permitted it. The sudden acquisition of ten thousand pounds was the most
remarkable charm of the young lady to whom he was now rendering himself
agreeable; but Elizabeth, less clear-sighted perhaps in this case than
in Charlotte’s, did not quarrel with him for his wish of independence.
Nothing, on the contrary, could be more natural; and, while able to
suppose that it cost him a few struggles to relinquish her, she was
ready to allow it a wise and desirable measure for both, and could very
sincerely wish him happy.

All this was acknowledged to Mrs. Gardiner; and, after relating the
circumstances, she thus went on:--“I am now convinced, my dear aunt,
that I have never been much in love; for had I really experienced that
pure and elevating passion, I should at present detest his very name,
and wish him all manner of evil. But my feelings are not only cordial
towards _him_, they are even impartial towards Miss King. I cannot find
out that I hate her at all, or that I am in the least unwilling to think
her a very good sort of girl. There can be no love in all this. My
watchfulness has been effectual; and though I should certainly be a more
interesting object to all my acquaintance, were I distractedly in love
with him, I cannot say that I regret my comparative insignificance.
Importance may sometimes be purchased too dearly. Kitty and Lydia take
his defection much more to heart than I do. They are young in the ways
of the world, and not yet open to the mortifying conviction that
handsome young men must have something to live on as well as the
plain.”

source.event_description: Elizabeth reads Darcy’s letter and is forced to confront his explanation of both the Netherfield events and Wickham’s character, moving from immediate anger and disbelief into sustained doubt and investigation.
source.first_words: Elizabeth, when Mr. Darcy gave her
source.last_words: been well assured of his cousin’s corroboration.
source.verbatim_passage:
Elizabeth, when Mr. Darcy gave her the letter, did not expect it to
contain a renewal of his offers, she had formed no expectation at all of
its contents. But such as they were, it may be well supposed how eagerly
she went through them, and what a contrariety of emotion they excited.
Her feelings as she read were scarcely to be defined. With amazement did
she first understand that he believed any apology to be in his power;
and steadfastly was she persuaded, that he could have no explanation to
give, which a just sense of shame would not conceal. With a strong
prejudice against everything he might say, she began his account of
what had happened at Netherfield. She read with an eagerness which
hardly left her power of comprehension; and from impatience of knowing
what the next sentence might bring, was incapable of attending to the
sense of the one before her eyes. His belief of her sister’s
insensibility she instantly resolved to be false; and his account of the
real, the worst objections to the match, made her too angry to have any
wish of doing him justice. He expressed no regret for what he had done
which satisfied her; his style was not penitent, but haughty. It was all
pride and insolence.

But when this subject was succeeded by his account of Mr. Wickham--when
she read, with somewhat clearer attention, a relation of events which,
if true, must overthrow every cherished opinion of his worth, and which
bore so alarming an affinity to his own history of himself--her feelings
were yet more acutely painful and more difficult of definition.
Astonishment, apprehension, and even horror, oppressed her. She wished
to discredit it entirely, repeatedly exclaiming, “This must be false!
This cannot be! This must be the grossest falsehood!”--and when she had
gone through the whole letter, though scarcely knowing anything of the
last page or two, put it hastily away, protesting that she would not
regard it, that she would never look in it again.

In this perturbed state of mind, with thoughts that could rest on
nothing, she walked on; but it would not do: in half a minute the letter
was unfolded again; and collecting herself as well as she could, she
again began the mortifying perusal of all that related to Wickham, and
commanded herself so far as to examine the meaning of every sentence.
The account of his connection with the Pemberley family was exactly
what he had related himself; and the kindness of the late Mr. Darcy,
though she had not before known its extent, agreed equally well with his
own words. So far each recital confirmed the other; but when she came to
the will, the difference was great. What Wickham had said of the living
was fresh in her memory; and as she recalled his very words, it was
impossible not to feel that there was gross duplicity on one side or the
other, and, for a few moments, she flattered herself that her wishes did
not err. But when she read and re-read, with the closest attention, the
particulars immediately following of Wickham’s resigning all pretensions
to the living, of his receiving in lieu so considerable a sum as three
thousand pounds, again was she forced to hesitate. She put down the
letter, weighed every circumstance with what she meant to be
impartiality--deliberated on the probability of each statement--but with
little success. On both sides it was only assertion. Again she read on.
But every line proved more clearly that the affair, which she had
believed it impossible that any contrivance could so represent as to
render Mr. Darcy’s conduct in it less than infamous, was capable of a
turn which must make him entirely blameless throughout the whole.

The extravagance and general profligacy which he scrupled not to lay to
Mr. Wickham’s charge exceedingly shocked her; the more so, as she could
bring no proof of its injustice. She had never heard of him before his
entrance into the ----shire militia, in which he had engaged at the
persuasion of the young man, who, on meeting him accidentally in town,
had there renewed a slight acquaintance. Of his former way of life,
nothing had been known in Hertfordshire but what he told

himself. As to his real character, had information been in her power,
she had never felt a wish of inquiring. His countenance, voice, and
manner, had established him at once in the possession of every virtue.
She tried to recollect some instance of goodness, some distinguished
trait of integrity or benevolence, that might rescue him from the
attacks of Mr. Darcy; or at least, by the predominance of virtue, atone
for those casual errors, under which she would endeavour to class what
Mr. Darcy had described as the idleness and vice of many years’
continuance. But no such recollection befriended her. She could see him
instantly before her, in every charm of air and address, but she could
remember no more substantial good than the general approbation of the
neighbourhood, and the regard which his social powers had gained him in
the mess. After pausing on this point a considerable while, she once
more continued to read. But, alas! the story which followed, of his
designs on Miss Darcy, received some confirmation from what had passed
between Colonel Fitzwilliam and herself only the morning before; and at
last she was referred for the truth of every particular to Colonel
Fitzwilliam himself--from whom she had previously received the
information of his near concern in all his cousin’s affairs and whose
character she had no reason to question. At one time she had almost
resolved on applying to him, but the idea was checked by the awkwardness
of the application, and at length wholly banished by the conviction that
Mr. Darcy would never have hazarded such a proposal, if he had not been
well assured of his cousin’s corroboration.

source.verbatim_passage:
When Jane and Elizabeth were alone, the former, who had been cautious in
her praise of Mr. Bingley before, expressed to her sister how very much
she admired him.

“He is just what a young-man ought to be,” said she, “sensible,
good-humoured, lively; and I never saw such happy manners! so much ease,
with such perfect good breeding!”

“He is also handsome,” replied Elizabeth, “which a young man ought
likewise to be if he possibly can. His character is thereby complete.”

“I was very much flattered by his asking me to dance a second time. I
did not expect such a compliment.”

“Did not you? _I_ did for you. But that is one great difference between
us. Compliments always take _you_ by surprise, and _me_ never. What
could be more natural than his asking you again? He could not help
seeing that you were about five times as pretty as every other woman in
the room. No thanks to his gallantry for that. Well, he certainly is
very agreeable, and I give you leave to like him. You have liked many a
stupider person.”

“Dear Lizzy!”

“Oh, you are a great deal too apt, you know, to like people in general.
You never see a fault in anybody. All the world are good and agreeable
in your eyes. I never heard you speak ill of a human being in my life.”

“I would wish not to be hasty in censuring anyone; but I always speak
what I think.”

“I know you do: and it is _that_ which makes the wonder. With _your_
good sense, to be so honestly blind to the follies and nonsense of
others! Affectation of candour is common enough; one meets with it
everywhere. But to be candid without ostentation or design,--to take the
good of everybody’s character and make it still better, and say nothing
of the bad,--belongs to you alone. And so, you like this man’s sisters,
too, do you? Their manners are not equal to his.”

“Certainly not, at first; but they are very pleasing women when you
converse with them. Miss Bingley is to live with her brother, and keep
his house; and I am much mistaken if we shall not find a very charming
neighbour in her.”

Elizabeth listened in silence, but was not convinced: their behaviour at
the assembly had not been calculated to please in general; and with more
quickness of observation and less pliancy of temper than her sister, and
with a judgment, too, unassailed by any attention to herself, she was
very little disposed to approve them. They were, in fact, very fine
ladies; not deficient in good-humour when they were pleased, nor in the
power of being agreeable where they chose it; but proud and conceited.
They were rather handsome; had been educated in one of the first private
seminaries in town; had a fortune of twenty thousand pounds; were in the
habit of spending more than they ought, and of associating with people
of rank; and were, therefore, in every respect entitled to think well of
themselves and meanly of others. They were of a respectable family in
the north of England; a circumstance more deeply impressed on their
memories than that their brother’s fortune and their own had been
acquired by trade.

source.note: The scenario matches the private post-assembly conversation between Jane and Elizabeth, and the anchor accurately reflects Elizabeth’s affectionate teasing, praise of Jane’s looks, and mild challenge to Jane’s charitable view of others, with the quoted line appearing verbatim.
